 Infantino re-election backed by South American football bloc 







BARRANQUILLA, Colombia (AFP)—FIFA president Gianni Infantino has “unanimous” backing for reelection as head of world football from CONMEBOL, the ten-country South American bloc said Friday.

Infantino faced criticism over his aborted plan to allow private investment into the World Cup, but he also retains support from Africa and Asia for his bid to win re-election next March.

Each country has one vote with 211 members and the winner will need to secure at least 106 votes in the ballot scheduled for March 18 in Rabat.

Conmebol has 10, Africa has 54 and Asia 46.

The CONMEBOL statement was made at Barranquilla ahead of Saturday’s Copa Sudamericana final between Brazil’s Atletico Mineiro and Argentina’s Boca Juniors.

CONMEBOL said it appreciated “the leadership of the current FIFA president” and the “positive transformations in football” that he has driven since taking office in 2016.

Having been the sole candidate in 2019 and 2023, Infantino faces two declared challengers: Frenchman Philippe Diallo and Japan’s Kozo Tashima.

Infantino has fended off criticism of the enlargement of the World Cup, giving a FIFA peace prize to Donald Trump and — at the American president’s request — overturning a red card for a US player during the competition.

So Infantino is under severe pressure for the first time, but mainly due to UEFA’s reaction to the private investor plan that forced his humiliating climbdown.

UEFA president Aleksander Ceferin has given full backing to Diallo, while Tashima has pledged to restore “integrity” to world football’s governing body.

Tashima, who serves on the FIFA Council, stressed his intention to restore trust in the governing body and make transparency and integrity the hallmarks of his campaign.

He said he decided to run after he was incensed by FIFA’s shock decision to lift the ban on United States player Folarin Balogun.

In October FIFA confirmed its intention to set up a $6.35-billion development fund for the next four years.

The fund would allow money to be distributed to FIFA’s 211 federations as well as to the regional confederations after a commercially successful 2026 World Cup.

The plan would allow for the payment of $25 million to all 211 member federations.

news.title: Zelensky says Putin is a 'killer' after Trump calls Russian leader a friend
news.text:
Zelensky called the attack the "biggest this year" and said the country suffered civilian deaths and injuries after an onslaught of 110 missiles, including 27 ballistic, and more than 400 drones.

Hours after the strikes on Ukraine, Trump told reporters at the White House that Putin would "love to end the war".

"They (Zelensky and Putin) both want to end it and it's a very good thing I have a relationship," he said on Friday.

Trump also doubled down on his description of the Russian leader as a friend but said he "can't speak" to whether Putin is a friend to the US.

However Zelensky said despite Trump's stance, he saw Putin as "a killer".

"I think mostly for the people in the world, he is a killer because he's killing - by the way- he's killing each day and night," he said.

Zelensky also said speaking about Putin like he is a "friend" means "he doesn't feel enough pressure". 

The war of words came as neighbouring Poland said a Russian cruise missile was among three objects that violated its airspace in the southeast of the country early on Friday.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said it did not appear to be an accident when Western military exercises were taking place in the region.

Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow.

Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned "grave violations of Polish airspace" and said Nato jets had been scrambled in response.

Russia has made no comment about the violations, which took place during Friday's massive attack on Ukraine. 

Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said one missile hit a rural area at Nowy Lipowiec about 50km (31 miles) from the Ukrainian border.

The missile hit about 100km (62 miles) from where European troops - from 11 of the 36 member nations of the Coalition of the Winning - were completing a training exercise, Polish authorities said. Another missile and a jet-powered drone were suspected to have hit two other locations, they added.
news.summary: Trump's comments came as Russia launched "biggest attacks this year" against Ukraine.

news.title: All the false and misleading claims Trump made after his Asia trip
news.text:
President Donald Trump made multiple false and misleading claims Friday at a news conference to discuss his recent trip to Asia. 

The president called his trip “one of the most successful presidential visits to Asia in American history,” discussing his meetings with leaders including Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

During the nearly 90-minute news conference, he embellished his achievements on subjects such as the economy, immigration and crime. 

Some claims were new, while others he has repeated constantly throughout his second administration.

Here's a closer look at the facts.

CLAIM: “Gasoline is down 60 cents a gallon from one month ago, and it's going to be dropping fast, and soon you'll have very, very low prices. When I was in Iowa, as I told the story, it was $1.85 a gallon” before the Iran war.

THE FACTS: Trump was arguing that gas prices were low before the war in Iran as a way of suggesting he had fulfilled a campaign promise to bring down everyday costs. But this claim about Iowa, which he made at an October rally in the state's conservative northwest, defies records kept by the American Automobile Association.

Iowa’s statewide average was $2.63 a gallon for regular gasoline on Feb. 27, 2026, the day before the Iran war began, according to AAA figures. The national average was $2.98.

The AAA says $3.69 is currently the national average price for a gallon of regular gasoline, compared to $4.27 a month ago. That's a drop of about 58 cents. However, prices remain 56 cents higher per gallon nationally than when Trump took office. He repeatedly said throughout campaign season that gas prices would come down after the election.

CLAIM: “Crude oil prices have plummeted right since the end of the election. I wonder how that happened. Crude oil is down 20% since the start of November, and now it’s down to close to $80 a barrel. And one of the largest drops, they say, in the history of oil.”

THE FACTS: Oil prices have fallen 20% since the election, a sharp decline in such a short period. Trump’s claim that it is “one of” the largest drops in history is imprecise. Over longer periods there have been much larger declines. For example, from July-December 2008, oil prices fell 79%.

According to the most commonly cited U.S. measure, oil prices were about $83.50 a barrel Friday and still almost 23% higher than they were just before the Iran war.

CLAIM: “We have had 10 straight months of manufacturing growth, which is a record. Investment in new equipment is up an incredible 21% this year.”

THE FACTS: It’s true that according to a monthly survey of manufacturers by the Institute for Supply Management, American factories as a whole report that they have grown for 10 months straight. But that’s nowhere near a record — the survey recorded 35 straight months of growth from September 2016 through July 2019, which is the record.

Another measure of factory output compiled by the Federal Reserve found that manufacturing production grew for nine of the past 10 months, falling only in August.

Most of the improvement in manufacturing stems from the artificial intelligence build-out, which has spurred demand for electrical components, HVAC equipment, wiring and other goods. The data center buildout also depends on the import of semiconductors, which have been exempted from tariffs.

CLAIM: “Crime is way down under the Trump administration, to the lowest levels in 100 — murder is down to the lowest level in 125 years, the year 1900.”

THE FACTS: The U.S. homicide rate dropped to the lowest it's been in 75 years, according to an FBI report on 2025 crime statistics released in August. It came close to beating the record, reaching 4.1 homicides per 100,000 people. The rate is tied with 1955 and 1956, according to August’s report, as the lowest rate since 1900.

But this drop is not due solely to the Trump administration. Experts say national violent crime rates have been declining since 2022, and pinpointing an exact reason is difficult. They say multiple factors contribute to decreases in crime rates seen in the FBI report, which is based on data reported voluntarily by many but not all law enforcement agencies across the country.

CLAIM: “We’ve created $25 trillion in new wealth since I took office. Twenty-five trillion with a T.”

THE FACTS: Trump has presented no evidence that he’s secured this much domestic or foreign investment in the U.S. Based on statements from various companies, foreign countries and the White House’s own website, that figure appears to be exaggerated, highly speculative and far higher than the actual sum. The White House website offers a far lower number, $11.4 trillion, and that figure appears to include some investment commitments made during the Biden administration.

CLAIM: “I did eight of those," saying he ended wars.

THE FACTS: Trump regularly says he has ended eight wars. Although he has helped mediate relations among many nations, his impact isn’t as clear-cut as he makes it seem. In at least two instances where he claims to have ended a war, there were no wars to end. He also began the ongoing war between the U.S. and Iran.

CLAIM: Somewhere between “30, 25 million came in under Biden over a four-year period."

THE FACTS: That figure, which Trump often cites in reference to people who entered the U.S. illegally, is highly inflated. U.S. Customs and Border Protection reports more than 10 million arrests for illegal crossings from Mexico from January 2021 through September 2024. That’s arrests, not people. 

Under pandemic-era asylum restrictions, many people crossed more than once until they succeeded because there were no legal consequences for getting turned back to Mexico. So the number of people is lower than the number of arrests.
news.summary: The president called his trip ’one of the most successful presidential visits to Asia in American history’
news.author: Melissa Goldin

news.title: Russia dusts off its prewar demands as the US raises discussing European security at Ukraine talks
news.text:
After nearly five years of fighting in Ukraine, the Kremlin is eagerly embracing a U.S. offer to discuss postwar European security, and Moscow is using that diplomatic opening to reaffirm the tough demands that President Vladimir Putin put forward before the start of his full-scale invasion.

The proposal to discuss broader security arrangements for Europe was floated by U.S. President Donald Trump’s envoys, and that has worried Ukraine and its Western allies, who fear it will play into Moscow’s hands and weaken NATO.

The Kremlin strongly backed the U.S. idea, describing a review of the broader European security framework as vital for a settlement of Europe’s most devastating conflict since World War II.

Putin discussed the Ukrainian conflict with Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen, China, their first trilateral meeting. That encounter had fueled fears in Ukraine that they could discuss a possible settlement without Kyiv's participation.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wants a ceasefire to include a security framework to ensure that Russia does not attack his country again, and European leaders argue that such an architecture already exists in the form of NATO.

 Russia's demands date back to 2021 

In draft agreements submitted to the U.S. and NATO in December 2021, two months before the invasion, Russia demanded that Washington and its allies pledge to exclude NATO’s expansion to Ukraine, Georgia or any other nation that was once part of the Soviet Union.

Moscow also demanded that the U.S. and its allies make a commitment to not deploy weapons or conduct any military activities in Ukraine and other ex-Soviet nations.

The documents also obliged the alliance not to station any troops in areas where they weren’t present in 1997 — before NATO moved to incorporate former Soviet bloc countries and ex-Soviet republics.

They also suggested a freeze on patrols by Russian and U.S. warships and bombers near each other’s borders. In addition, they called for efforts to reduce the risk of incidents involving Russia and NATO warships and aircraft, primarily in the Baltic and the Black seas; a reduction in the scope of military drills; and greater transparency and other confidence-building measures.

NATO allies have rejected the Russian demands as a nonstarter.

Putin described the West's refusal to consider these proposals as the main reason behind his decision to send troops into Ukraine on Feb. 24, 2022, arguing that he had to act to fend off a major threat to Russia's national security. Ukraine and its allies denounce the invasion as an unprovoked act of aggression.

 Moscow sees an opportunity to revive and expand its demands 

Speaking after the meeting with Xi and Trump, Putin reaffirmed his criticism of the West for failing to take Moscow's complaints about NATO's expansion into account.

"They just spat at our opinion,” he said.

Putin bluntly rejected the European response to Moscow's plans. He called it “political diarrhea” and “nonsense,” saying that “everybody understands that we don't strive for a war with Europe.”

He said Russia is open to discussing the continent's security arrangements with the Europeans as the U.S. has suggested, and scoffed at “hysterics in some European capitals" over Washington's offer.

“We understand that it makes no sense to discuss issues related to security in Europe without the Europeans,” Putin declared. He said Moscow invited a European delegation to visit and state its negotiating position before deciding on the date and format of Ukrainian talks.

Russia is ready to search for compromise, he said, but will not budge on its key demands. He has sternly warned that Russia will not accept the deployment of any European troops into Ukraine after the hostilities end and see them as a legitimate target.

Kremlin foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov said that during talks with Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner on Nov. 12 in the Kremlin, Putin reminded them of Moscow's 2021 security proposals, noting that they envisioned the pullback of NATO forces from Central and Eastern Europe.

Ushakov said the Kremlin would now update them with “fresh considerations.”

 Some see room for compromise by Russia 

While Putin appears adamant on keeping Kyiv out of NATO and blocking any Western troops on Ukrainian soil, some observers say Moscow could be open to concessions on its other demands, including the rollback of NATO troops from Central and Eastern Europe.

Alexei Naumov, a pro-Kremlin political commentator, argued that Russian demands represented an initial bargaining position that could become more flexible during talks.

“Between maintaining the current status quo and the full realization of Russia’s demands, there is a vast space for compromise: mutual arms limitations, agreements regarding the deployment of military infrastructure, the parameters for a future Ukrainian military, security guarantees, and mechanisms to monitor their implementation,” he said in a commentary.

“Russia is currently negotiating from a position of strength, but that does not at all mean there will be no compromises.”

Tatiana Stanovaya, an expert at the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center, said that “for the first time since 2022, Moscow sees a concrete opening for negotiations that could address what it calls the ‘root causes’ of the war.”

“The Kremlin thinks the opportunity is worth pursuing, even though its expectations for this round are low,” she said. “If the talks fail, Russia is prepared to keep fighting until another opening presents itself.”

Russia expert Mark Galeotti, who heads the Mayak Intelligence consultancy, said Moscow’s set of demands could reflect “the classic attempt to start with a very, very exaggeratedly ambitious list of proposals with the expectation that you get haggled down.”

Putin could be searching for a face-saving way to end the war without achieving the land gains in Ukraine that he had sought, Galeotti noted in a recent podcast.

 Ukraine and its allies fear security talks will benefit Moscow 

European leaders fear that Putin could persuade Trump to support a peace settlement that would weaken not only Ukraine but broader European security.

The European Union’s top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, said Europe must insist on a ceasefire before taking the negotiations further — the opposite of what Putin demands.

“If we start to talk about what Russia is asking regarding the security architecture, we actually walk into the traps that Russia is setting us,” she said at a meeting of the European Political Community in Dublin earlier this month.

Zelenskyy also has warned that the U.S. proposal to discuss a new security framework for Europe before the war’s end could be dangerous, arguing that Moscow could use such discussions to weaken NATO and reshape the continent’s borders.

Kushner, meanwhile, said after meeting with Zelenskyy and European leaders on Thursday in Berlin that Trump wants to make a deal with Europe “by his side” and is not looking to impose a unilateral agreement. He also emphasized that Trump is “open” to NATO-like security guarantees for postwar Ukraine, added that he believes Russia is “comfortable” with the allies offering such assurances to Kyiv.

Trump called into the Berlin talks following his meeting with Putin, Kushner said.

Stanovaya noted that Putin wants Europe to accept that Russia will have to be part of any negotiation on European security and predicted that the prospective talks will fuel differences among the allies.

“I expect the process to deepen divisions within Europe, with little prospect of concrete results,” she said in a post on X.
news.summary: After nearly five years of fighting in Ukraine, the Kremlin is eagerly embracing a U.S. offer to discuss postwar European security

news.title: Donald Trump’s Yalta Lite
news.text:
Donald Trump walked down the stairs of Air Force One in Shenzhen on 18 November to a predictably extravagant welcome. A military guard stood at attention, bayonets gleaming. Performers waved flowers and flags, chanting “warm welcome” in unison. Xi Jinping was waiting to greet Trump on a red carpet at the base of the steps. The two men hugged and watched a formation of fighter jets streak overhead in Trump’s honour. Xi said he was merely reciprocating the gracious welcome he received in Washington in September, but the Chinese leader has long since mastered the art of playing to Trump’s insatiable desire for spectacle.

The reason for this gathering was nominally the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit, but the main event was always going to be the historic trilateral between Trump, Xi, and Vladimir Putin on 19 November – the first ever such meeting between the leaders of the United States, China, and Russia. They met at a secluded villa inside the Kylin Resort – a lakeside compound outside Shenzhen that has previously hosted the late North Korean leader, Kim Jong Il, and Xi’s own father, Xi Zhongxun. The three leaders took their seats around a circular wooden table, beneath a vast painting of a beautiful mountain scene, nominally as equals, but with the official photographs making clear that it was Xi, seated in the centre, who was in charge.
news.summary: The president’s insatiable desire for spectacle has handed a victory to Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping

news.title: Union Minister Rijiju poses four questions to Cong over LoP Gandhi’s remarks; seeks apology for ‘1962 war humiliation’
news.text:
New Delhi: Union Minister Kiren Rijiju Saturday launched a fresh attack on the Congress, posing four questions to the party, including whether it would apologise for the “1962 war humiliation” and why it kept India a “poor nation”.

In a post on X, Union Minister Rijiju listed four questions for the Congress and called on the party to respond to them.

“My village was occupied by China in 1962. Will Congress apologise for the 1962 humiliation?” he asked, referring to the India-China war.

Union Minister Rijiju questioned, “Congress kept India a poor nation. Why?”

He also sought an explanation from the Opposition party over why India was described as the “land of snake charmers”.

“Why was India’s economy insulted as Hindu rate of growth?” the Union Minister asked.

Union Minister Rijiju’s remarks came after Leader of Opposition (LoP) in the Lok Sabha, Rahul Gandhi criticised Prime Minister Narendra Modi over a trilateral meeting involving US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China Thursday.

Taking a swipe at the Prime Minister, LoP Gandhi had said that India would have been represented at the high-level meeting if the Congress were in power.

“If Congress were in power, India’s Prime Minister would be sitting at this table. A compromised PM can never sit at this table,” LoP Gandhi wrote in a post on X.

Union Minister Rijiju also criticised LoP Gandhi while speaking to reporters Friday, saying that the Congress leader should refrain from making statements against India, whether within the country or during his visits abroad.

The Union Minister accused LoP Gandhi of “colluding with foreign-based anti-India forces” and spreading what he termed “falsehoods” about India’s democracy and the state of its economy.

“It is also possible that anti-India forces abroad and across the world keep provoking him (Rahul Gandhi). He has himself developed an anti-India mindset, focussing on how to undermine India, its civilisation, traditions, democracy and the Constitution. Rahul Gandhi has already opened a front against these institutions,” Rijiju alleged.

news.title: US should explicitly state its desire to enter into peace agreement with Iran — Araghchi
news.text:
TEHRAN, November 21. /TASS/. The United States must change its position and state a clear intention to reach a peace agreement with Iran in order to begin negotiations on opening the Strait of Hormuz, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said in an interview with the newspaper Iran.

"We have not received any response from the American side. Therefore, if they are truly serious about reaching an agreement, it is only natural that we would first expect them to change their position," he said, commenting on a recent statement by US leader Donald Trump that the United States no longer needs a deal with the republic.

Tehran is demanding that Washington explicitly state its desire to conclude a peace agreement and adopt a set of confidence-building measures between the two sides, the minister added. If the American side fulfills these two conditions, Iran is prepared to discuss the draft agreement and its implementation, he noted.

"Our demand is perfectly clear: for the Strait of Hormuz to be opened, seven conditions we have put forward must be met. Of course, if the Americans have any proposals or opinions regarding the fulfillment of these conditions, we are prepared to discuss them. If Iran’s demands are met, the Strait of Hormuz will be opened. Even if it becomes necessary to discuss the details and ways to implement these conditions, we are ready to enter into negotiations at the expert level," Araghchi stressed.

Iran is also prepared for negotiations regarding its enriched uranium stockpiles, he said, adding though that Tehran insists that nuclear materials must not leave the country.
news.summary: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi noted Tehran is also prepared for negotiations regarding its enriched uranium stockpiles

news.title: Trump, Putin and Xi Unveil 4-Point Declaration After Historic Summit
news.text:
President Donald Trump joined Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in issuing a joint “peace declaration” Thursday after the three leaders met on the sidelines of the 2026 Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders’ Meeting in Shenzhen, China.

“The three heads of state had an in-depth exchange of views on the current international situation and committed to maintaining strategic stability and international security,” the White House said in a statement titled “U.S.-Russia-China Heads of State Declaration toward Peace.” 

Russia’s Foreign Ministry and China’s Chamber of Commerce to the EU released statements that closely mirrored the White House account. The documents emphasized cooperation on limiting nuclear proliferation, expanding global petroleum production and supporting international institutions.

“The three countries plan to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations. They reaffirmed the importance of stable energy flows,” the U.S., Chinese and Russian statements said.

China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs issued a longer account of the leaders’ discussions.

“President Xi noted that it is a groundbreaking move for the top leaders of China, Russia and the United States to hold the first-ever meeting in history. History tells us that peace among major countries brings stability to the world, while their contention would only lead to chaos in the world. Peace has been an enduring pursuit of humanity,” the statement said.

Chinese officials described the historic gathering—the first time the leaders of the three countries have met together—as focused on “Safeguarding World Peace and Promoting Strategic Stability in Major-Country Relations.”

“More than 80 years ago, China, Russia and the United States, the key anti-fascist forces in the world, fought shoulder to shoulder and achieved great victories, winning peace and tranquility for the world. History is the best textbook; we must remember history, and learn from it to shape the future,” the statement added.

The three governments also pledged to reduce the risk of nuclear conflict. Each statement included the declaration that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought.”

China’s account also said Trump recognized the international attention surrounding the summit.

“President Trump noted that the U.S.-China-Russia summit draws attention from across the world. It is very important and has made history. The three countries are all nuclear-weapon states, and have a special and important responsibility to safeguard world peace and stability,” the statement said.

A separate Chinese readout identified several issues discussed by the leaders, including Russia’s war in Ukraine, continuing tensions in the Middle East and the situation on the Korean Peninsula.

China characterized the three-way summit as “positive, constructive and very productive.”

“President Xi emphasized that the seeds sown at the summit today among the three presidents will surely take root, sprout, bloom and bear fruit,” the statement concluded.

news.title: Trump orders federal contractors to notify White House before giving Congress information
news.text:
President Donald Trump on Friday ordered companies with federal contracts to alert the White House before sharing information with Congress and withhold material the administration deems confidential, expanding his efforts to limit congressional oversight before Democrats take control of Congress in January.

Trump’s executive order, issued late on Friday, applies to federal contractors and their subcontractors. Companies that fail to comply could face cancellation of existing contracts or suspension from future federal business, it said.

The order is part of a broader effort by the Republican president to control what information reaches Congress and limit Democratic investigations into his administration, setting up a potentially significant battle over presidential power and lawmakers’ authority to scrutinize the White House.

Democrats, who won control of both chambers of Congress in this month’s midterm elections, have vowed to investigate Trump’s administration, his family’s business dealings and its relationships with private companies.

Friday’s order follows a directive issued this week by White House Counsel Will Scharf requiring federal agencies to obtain White House approval before employees agree to testify before Congress. Scharf said certain Democratic investigations could amount to criminal conduct, a claim that has raised questions about the administration’s attempts to limit congressional oversight.

The restrictions could face legal challenges, particularly if contractors are told to withhold information sought through congressional subpoenas. Executive privilege allows presidents to protect certain confidential communications, but courts can intervene in disputes over Congress’ authority to obtain information.

Democrats are preparing to investigate potential conflicts of interest, federal contracts, immigration enforcement and the administration’s handling of the Jeffrey Epstein investigation. Representative Robert Garcia of California, who is set to lead the House Oversight Committee, this week asked 12 of Trump’s top allies, former aides and family members to preserve documents related to alleged Trump family corruption and government misconduct.

Garcia’s letters, sent to Trump’s relatives, White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, Vice President JD Vance, Attorney General Todd Blanche and former White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, among others, laid the groundwork for Democratic lawmakers’ oversight investigations.

The offices of Garcia, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and Senator Elizabeth Warren, the ranking Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee, did not respond to requests for comment on Friday night.

The White House defended Friday’s order as necessary to protect sensitive government communications, including those involving national security. It said contractors responding independently to congressional requests could expose privileged information and force the administration into costly legal disputes.

Trump’s Justice Department has also argued that executive privilege can extend to communications between the president and outside advisers, even if those advisers do not work for the government.

news.title: Trump says Putin wants talks to end Ukraine war
news.text:
Washington: US President Donald Trump said that Russian President Vladimir Putin had told him in Shenzhen he wanted a diplomatic end to the war in Ukraine. Pressed on why he believed Putin after a reporter cited a fresh Russian attack, Trump said both leaders wanted the fighting to stop but saw no way out.

Trump met Putin Thursday after addressing leaders of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum in China. He said Putin “clearly expressed his desire to see the war between Russia and Ukraine end by diplomatic means”. Trump announced no ceasefire, date for negotiations or terms that Moscow was prepared to offer Kyiv.

At a White House news conference on his return from Asia, a reporter asked how Trump could be sure Putin was acting in good faith. The reporter said the Russian leader had left their meeting and launched another deadly assault on Ukraine. Trump stood by his assessment of Putin and said the US was trying to help both sides find a way to end the war.

He identified the hostility between Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky as a particular obstacle. “The problem is President Zelensky and President Putin have tremendous hatred, and it’s never easy,” he said.

Trump said he had initially thought the war would be among the easier conflicts for him to settle. He had since spoken to US representatives involved in the diplomatic effort and believed an agreement was still possible. He put the monthly death toll at about 25,000, most of them soldiers. He gave no source for that estimate.

Asked separately whether he considered Putin a friend to the United States, Trump confined his answer to his own dealings with the Russian leader. He said it was in the American interest for a president to be able to speak directly to the head of a country with one of the world’s largest nuclear arsenals.

Trump cited his first administration’s decision to supply Ukraine with Javelin anti-tank missiles in answer to criticism that he was too accommodating towards Moscow. On current US weapons supplies, he said European buyers paid for American equipment and passed much of it on to Ukraine.

Ukraine also came up when Chinese President Xi Jinping joined Trump and Putin for a three-way meeting in Shenzhen. Trump said the leaders discussed how to stop the killing. The specific undertaking he reported from that meeting concerned nuclear weapons. China, he said, had agreed to talks with Washington and Moscow on reducing nuclear risk. He described no agreement among the three on Ukraine.

Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, eight years after seizing and annexing Crimea. Zelenskyy, who took office in 2019, has led Ukraine throughout the full-scale war. The supply of Javelin missiles that Trump cited dates to his first term, when Ukrainian forces were already fighting Russian-backed separatists in the east of the country.

news.title: Trump hails India's 7% GDP growth, low interest rates as he lambasts US Fed Reserve
news.text:
US President Donald Trump praised India's relatively low interest rate and 7 per cent economic growth as he launched a blistering attack on the American central bank. He accused the Federal Reserve of “destroying the country" by raising interest rates whenever the United States posts strong financial numbers.
The remarks from the American leader came while he was conducting a press briefing in the White House on Friday. He was flanked by US Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. While speaking to reporters, Trump argued that the US should have the lowest interest rates in the world. He pointed to India's economic momentum as a model. He went on to claim that cutting borrowing costs would allow US gross domestic product (GDP) to surge far beyond its current pace.
He drew a comparison between New Delhi's monetary environment and that of Washington. Trump argued that strong economic indicators should be rewarded with cheaper credit rather than tighter policy.
“If you look at India, they have low interest rates, and they have a 7 per cent GDP. We would have a 14, 15, or maybe even a 20 per cent GDP. It’s really a sad thing when you do so well, and then they raise the interest rate. The fact is, we’ve blown through it," Trump said.
'Very political'
He noted that a faster-growing economy makes the United States a stronger credit risk and would enable his administration to pay down the national debt rapidly. Trump claimed that every single percentage point in interest rates represents $650 billion.
While expressing his anger over high interest rates, the American president described the Federal Reserve as a "very political" entity. He alleged that policymakers deliberately hike rates when positive economic data is released to cool momentum.
Despite the Federal Reserve's stance, Trump insisted that his tariff policies are driving a domestic manufacturing boom, claiming thousands of factories are being built across the United States even in the face of high borrowing costs.

news.title: Strait of Hormuz Latest: Tanker Struck Near Oman as Traffic Stays Far Below Normal and Iran Keeps Its Grip
news.text: A tanker caught fire near the Strait of Hormuz on Friday after being struck off the coast of Oman. The incident underscored how dangerous the world's most important oil chokepoint remains, nearly nine months after the conflict with Iran began.The U.K. Maritime Trade Operations agency, which monitors shipping security in the region, said an outbound tanker was hit by an unknown projectile about 8 nautical miles north of Khasab, Oman. The ship caught fire. No casualties or environmental damage were reported.Iran's Revolutionary Guards gave a different account, saying the tanker had struck a mine. The cause could not be independently verified.Iranian media also reported that a missile struck Qeshm Island, an Iranian island inside the strait. Details on that incident were limited.How the crisis beganThe strait, a narrow passage between Iran and Oman that normally carries about a fifth of the world's oil, has been at the center of the conflict since Feb. 28, 2026, when the United States and Israel launched strikes on Iran. Tehran responded by closing the waterway to what it called "hostile" shipping.Iran has since required ships to obtain transit permits through a body it calls the Persian Gulf Strait Authority. On Nov. 10, Iranian officials said the strait would not reopen until the United States meets Tehran's conditions.US says routes are clearWashington has pushed back. U.S. Central Command said on Oct. 25 that the main shipping lanes had been cleared of mines and that more than 3,000 vessels had crossed with U.S. support.President Donald Trump has said the military campaign is effectively over and that Navy escorts are working. A third U.S. aircraft carrier has now arrived in the region, according to market and media reports.Traffic numbers tell a mixed storyHow much shipping is actually moving depends on which data source is used.The International Monetary Fund's PortWatch tracker recorded just two transits on Nov. 15, against a pre-crisis baseline of about 85 a day.The tracking site hormuz.now, which counts ships visible on the Automatic Identification System, shows an average of about 5.7 transits a day over the past week. That is roughly 7% of normal.UKMTO has estimated that overall traffic is running about 65% below pre-war levels.The gap appears to come largely from so-called "dark" transits. These are ships, often under U.S. escort, that switch off their tracking transponders to avoid being targeted. The advocacy group United Against Nuclear Iran has estimated that U.S.-facilitated dark transits averaged about 27.7 vessels a day.Human and financial costThe toll on seafarers has been heavy. The International Maritime Organization has counted 138 maritime incidents and 25 seafarer deaths in the region since the war began.The cost of passage has also climbed. U.S. official Hung Cao said this week that insurance for a single transit had reached $64 million, Al Jazeera reported.Those costs have pushed some shipowners to avoid the route entirely, while others rely on government-backed insurance and naval escorts.Market impactFriday's tanker fire helped lift oil prices off their lows. Brent crude settled at $92.57 a barrel, up 0.64%, though it still posted its third straight weekly loss as Gulf supplies continue to recover.Energy analysts say the market has become less sensitive to individual incidents than it was earlier in the year. Still, they warn that a major attack or a collapse in escort operations could quickly drive prices higher again.What comes nextThe near-term outlook remains uncertain. Iran has shown no sign of dropping its permit system, and the United States has not publicly accepted any of Tehran's conditions. Concerns about possible new U.S. strikes on Iran are adding to the tension.For shipping companies, the key questions are whether escorted traffic can keep growing and whether attacks like Friday's become more frequent. Maritime security agencies continue to urge vessels in the area to exercise caution and report any suspicious activity.

"If Congress were in power, India's Prime Minister would be sitting at this table. A compromised PM can never sit at this table," the Leader of the Opposition said.

His remarks drew a sharp response from the BJP, with Rijiju leading the counter-attack.
Rijiju Accuses Rahul Gandhi Of Undermining India's Image
Speaking to reporters on Friday, Rijiju urged Gandhi against making statements that could damage India's reputation, whether within the country or overseas.
The Union minister accused the Congress leader of "colluding with foreign-based anti-India forces" and spreading "falsehoods" about India's democracy and economic condition.
He further alleged that forces operating outside India could be encouraging Gandhi's criticism. Rijiju also accused the Congress leader of developing an anti-India mindset and attempting to undermine the country's civilisation, traditions, democratic institutions and Constitution.
The minister claimed Gandhi had already opened a front against these institutions.

BJP Leaders Target 'Side Player' Remark
Rijiju's attack comes amid a broader BJP offensive against Gandhi over his recent comments on India's standing in international affairs.
The Congress leader had described India as a "side player" in global geopolitics, arguing that the country had lost its ability to independently influence major international discussions.
He also questioned how Pakistan continued to engage with influential countries, including the United States and Iran, while India was allegedly losing diplomatic space.

news.title: Trump Calls Ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang ‘Brilliant’, Says He Deserves A ‘Second Chance’
news.text:
US President Donald Trump has voiced support for Jensen Huang's possible return to Nvidia, saying the former chief executive deserves another opportunity despite the controversy surrounding his exit from the chipmaker. Trump described Huang as one of the world's brightest minds and urged him to apologise before returning to the company he co-founded.
Speaking to reporters on Friday, Trump expressed his willingness to see Huang resume leadership at Nvidia, which plays a crucial role in the global artificial intelligence industry. "I think that I would love to see Jensen be given a second chance," Trump said. Describing Huang as "a good man" who "made some bad decisions", Trump added that he wanted the former CEO to issue an apology and return to the company.
"I'd like to see Jensen make a big apology and go back because he created something with Blackwell," he said, referring to Nvidia's advanced chip architecture.
Trump Raises Huang's Exit With Xi Jinping
Trump also indicated that he had discussed Huang's situation with Chinese President Xi Jinping during their summit earlier this week.
The US president's remarks appeared to differ from the position taken by his Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. Bessent had stressed that Washington must maintain its technological advantage over Beijing, particularly in artificial intelligence.
The developments come amid growing scrutiny of China's alleged attempts to access advanced American semiconductor technology.
ALSO READ: Trump Cites India's 7% GDP Growth To Slam 'Political' US Federal Reserve Over High Interest Rates
Alleged Chinese Spy Links Triggered Controversy
Huang's departure last week followed reports linking him to Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed International, who was reportedly suspected by US intelligence of having connections to Beijing.
According to reports, investigators examined whether Megaspeed had helped China obtain advanced Nvidia AI processors despite US export restrictions. The Chinese government has denied the allegations.
At least two other alleged affairs involving Huang reportedly emerged following the initial revelations.
Nvidia's board had initiated an independent investigation into whether its chief executive had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. The company maintained that it had no reason to believe its confidential information or US national security interests had been compromised.
Nvidia Board Rules Out Immediate Comeback
Despite Trump's public endorsement, Huang's return faces an obstacle within Nvidia itself. Chairman Harvey C. Jones said on November 17 that the board had no plans to reinstate the former chief executive.
Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress is currently serving as interim CEO as the company looks for a permanent successor.
Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and led the company for more than three decades. He acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife and apologised to his family and colleagues, while reiterating his commitment to the company and US national security.
He has also agreed to respond to questions from American lawmakers about the alleged Chinese intelligence connection and its implications for sensitive technology. He is expected to appear before the Senate Banking Committee and participate in a closed-door interview with House committees.
ALSO READ: 6.8-Magnitude Earthquake Strikes Central Peru, Residents Rush Onto Streets In Lima
Why Huang's Return Matters For Nvidia
Nvidia occupies a central position in the global AI race, with its processors powering the development and operation of advanced artificial intelligence systems.

news.title: Trump’s Asia trip: Key takeaways from his briefing
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Nov 20 (IANS) US President Donald Trump said China had agreed to nuclear-risk talks with Washington and Moscow, cited India's economic growth to press for lower US interest rates and set limits on how far he wanted the Quad to go in sharing advanced technology. Here are takeaways from his Friday news conference after returning from Asia. Trump said Chinese President Xi Jinping agreed in Shenzhen to discuss reducing nuclear risks with the US and Russia. The three leaders declared that nuclear conflict must never be allowed to happen, he said. They announced no timetable or arms cuts. Trump acknowledged he would find it difficult to agree to halve the US arsenal. India figured in Trump's case for a Fed rate cut as Trump pointed to what he described as New Delhi's low interest rates and 7 per cent growth. He argued that cheaper borrowing could lift US growth to 14 or 15 per cent, possibly even 20 per cent. He offered no calculation behind that projection. It was also announced that Quad companies would meet in early 2027. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said leading companies from India, the US, Japan and Australia would meet early next year to explore commercial deals. Prime Minister Narendra Modi attended the Quad summit in Manila, where leaders also agreed to cooperate on supply chains and maritime surveillance. Trump drew limits on AI cooperation. He said the Quad had launched an initiative on advanced artificial intelligence, but he wanted most of the development work kept in the US. He threatened a substantial tax on American companies building data centres abroad. Separately, he said he and Xi had agreed to work together on AI safeguards. The US President said that he would like Jensen Huang to apologise and return to Nvidia, although he had earlier recommended Tim Cook for the job. He credited Huang with developing Nvidia's Blackwell chips and said any American chips sold to China should be older models. Trump said Russian President Vladimir Putin had expressed a desire to end the Ukraine war at their meeting in Shenzhen. Challenged over a fresh Russian attack, Trump maintained that both leaders wanted the fighting to stop. He announced no ceasefire or negotiating date. Thailand and the Philippines featured in trade deals. Trump said Thailand had signed an agreement to eliminate tariffs on US goods and wanted to buy $2.6 billion in American farm products annually. He called that figure preliminary. Under a separate Philippine framework, he said he pressed Manila to buy all its agricultural and energy imports from the US. A Mexico deal drew closer, but Canada continues to face pressure. Trump said he was close to a deal after meeting Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum. He welcomed Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney's interest in the Keystone pipeline but said he wanted the US trade deficit with Canada, which he put at about $80 billion, reduced to zero. Trump would make the same decision on Iran. He acknowledged that the war had pushed up fuel prices but said preventing Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon justified his decision. Asked whether the war was worth Republicans losing the Senate, Vice President J.D. Vance defended that objective and said the decision was Trump's. Trump said Democrats had contacted him about immigration and health care. He expected them to raise the fate of people who entered the US unlawfully years ago and had since worked in the country. He made no commitment on whether they could stay.

news.title: Trump formally ends minting of the penny after nearly 250 years of production
news.text: Washington is officially done with spending a pretty penny on penny production. President Donald Trump on Friday signed the bipartisan Common Cents Act, which formally directs the federal government to stop minting the penny. Both the House and the Senate passed the measure by voice vote, meaning no notable opposition. “It costs nearly FOUR cents to make just one penny,” the bill’s author, Rep. Lisa McClain, R-Mich., said Sept. 29 on X a day after Senate passage. “This legislation will save $85 million per year by permanently ending penny production — it’s common sense!” The U.S. Mint last year put the immediate annual savings of discontinuing penny production at $56 million. The government stopped making pennies in November 2025, nine months after Trump called for the Treasury Department to stop production, writing at the time that the process was “so wasteful!” However, the U.S. Mint said it would still produce collector versions to be produced in “limited quantities.” The penny can still be used as legal tender “for all debts, public charges, taxes, and dues,” according to the new law. The Treasury Department said last year that the Federal Reserve will continue to recirculate the approximately 114 billion pennies that are in existence “for as long as possible.” The new measure also provides a procedure for stores and businesses that accept cash payments to round their prices to the nearest amount divisible by 5 cents. And, as the nickel replaces the penny at the bottom of the U.S. Mint’s currency list, that coin can now be manufactured with an inner layer of zinc and an outer layer of nickel. It is currently produced with nickel and copper, which costs more than zinc. Congress passed the Coinage Act in 1792, and the U.S. Mint began producing the penny, known officially as the cent, the following year. In its nearly 250 years in production, the penny has had multiple facades. It wasn’t until 1909 that it was given its modern-day face, featuring President Abraham Lincoln. The first penny, produced in 1787, had a sundial design created by Benjamin Franklin. After the U.S. Mint took over, the penny was slightly bigger and included the image of a woman representing Liberty on one side and 15 chain links on the other. The next penny debuted in 1857, taking on a smaller shape and displaying a flying eagle design on one side and a wreath on the other. It also changed from being 100% copper to 88% copper and 12% nickel. Two years later, an “Indian Head” design was added to one side. The most recent design from the U.S. Mint was issued in 2010, featuring its “Union Shield” theme. It shows a shield on the tails side of the coin to represent “Lincoln’s preservation of the United States as a single country,” the U.S. Mint wrote.
news.summary: The U.S. Mint, which began producing the currency in 1793, has said it costs nearly 4 cents to make each penny.
news.author: Kyla Guilfoil

news.title: As Trump Embraces Putin, Expert Urges Europe to Prepare for War Without US
news.text:
Europe must prepare to fight Russia without the US and establish a joint political and military “War Council” to coordinate its response, according to a new security analysis.

The warning comes as US President Donald Trump publicly embraced Russian President Vladimir Putin as a “friend” during their Nov. 19 summit in China, renewing questions about Washington’s relationship with Moscow and Europe’s ability to rely on American leadership in a security crisis.

In a November policy brief titled The War Council, Sven Biscop, research director at Belgium’s Egmont Institute and professor at Ghent University, argues that Europe’s greatest weakness is not its military or economic strength but its inability to make rapid, unified decisions during wartime.

He warns that Putin could exploit those divisions, potentially miscalculating that European governments would fail to respond effectively to an attack on NATO or EU territory.

Biscop’s assessment raises a fundamental question for European governments: If the US increasingly treats Russia as a diplomatic partner while European countries regard Moscow as their principal security threat, can Europe still assume Washington would respond to a Russian attack as it has in the past?

Biscop does not argue that the US has abandoned NATO. Rather, he insists that European governments must prepare for a situation in which American military participation is delayed or absent.

His proposal goes beyond increasing defense spending or acquiring additional weapons. Europe, he argues, needs a political command structure capable of coordinating military operations, economic mobilization, diplomacy and the wider demands of war.

NATO without the US: Europe must prepare to fight alone

One of Biscop’s most consequential warnings concerns the possibility that the US could decline to participate in a conventional European war, at least initially.

He identifies two scenarios: an American president who disagrees with Europe’s assessment of a threat, or a Washington administration whose military resources are already committed to a conflict in Asia.

Under either scenario, European governments would have to determine their own military objectives, organize their defenses and coordinate their broader response without waiting for Washington.

The argument marks a significant departure from Europe’s traditional reliance on American leadership within NATO.

Biscop distinguishes between the alliance’s existing military plans and the political decisions required to sustain a major war. NATO may be prepared to repel an initial invasion, but European leaders would still need to decide how far operations should extend, what political objectives they should pursue and how to mobilize their economies.

He also raises the question of identifying reliable partners beyond NATO and the EU, determining which countries would remain neutral and deciding how to approach governments whose interests might diverge from Europe’s.

Those concerns have acquired renewed significance following Trump’s meetings with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen.

Trump described Putin as his “friend” during their meeting Thursday and later praised his personal relationship with the Russian leader.

His remarks do not establish that Washington would refuse to defend a NATO ally. They do, however, provide a political backdrop to Biscop’s central argument: European defense planning must account for decisions in Washington that may not align with European security assessments.

Biscop previously warned Kyiv Post of a historic US-Europe rupture

Biscop’s latest proposal builds on warnings he delivered in an earlier interview with Kyiv Post on March 28, when he argued that the Trump administration’s relationship with Europe represented a fundamental change in transatlantic politics.

He said Washington increasingly regarded Europe as a geopolitical competitor rather than an automatic partner and warned that Ukraine could suffer the most immediate consequences of that shift.

Biscop also argued that Trump’s willingness to negotiate with Putin without European participation risked producing agreements at Ukraine’s expense.

His assessment of the American president’s geopolitical orientation was particularly pointed:

“I think Trump is closer to Putin than to Europe,” Biscop told Kyiv Post.

He warned that European leaders were increasingly recognizing the need for an independent defense capability, even while maintaining NATO as their preferred security framework.

At the time, Biscop said Europe needed contingency plans for a conflict in which American forces would not fight alongside European troops.

His November paper goes further by examining what European governments would actually need to do to conduct such a war, particularly when existing institutions divide responsibility among NATO, the EU and national governments.

The emphasis has shifted from whether Europe possesses enough military capabilities to whether it has the political machinery to use them effectively.

Who runs the war? Europe risks confusion and disaster

Biscop identifies what he considers a dangerous institutional vacuum: Europe has no single political body capable of directing a major war against a comparable military power.

He points to the response to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine as an example of how complicated European decision-making has become.

Military assistance and strategic decisions are divided among the European Union, NATO, the Ukraine Defense Contact Group, which includes the United States, and the Coalition of the Willing, which operates without Washington.

Each structure has different participants, powers and procedures.

Although this system has enabled Western countries to sustain considerable assistance to Kyiv, Biscop argues that it would be far more difficult to manage if European states were directly engaged in a large-scale war.

Such a confrontation would require governments to make immediate decisions about military operations, the movement of troops and supplies, weapons production, financial stability and relations with other countries.

Biscop argues that NATO’s military command structure cannot substitute for unified political leadership, particularly when many economic and industrial responsibilities fall under EU or national authority.

He therefore proposes linking NATO’s Article 5 collective defense mechanism with the EU’s Article 42.7 mutual assistance provision, allowing both institutions to mobilize their respective powers.

His broader concern is that Moscow could misinterpret Europe’s fragmented political structures as evidence that its member states would be unable to respond together.

That perception, he argues, could weaken deterrence even if Europe’s combined military and economic resources were sufficient to confront Russia.

‘Would Europe Have Enough Time?’ Lessons from World War II

To illustrate the dangers of preparing for war too late, Biscop draws a historical comparison between Britain and France during World War II.

Britain, he writes, required approximately a year to develop the political and military decision-making machinery needed to direct its war effort effectively.

It benefited from the English Channel, which prevented German ground forces from advancing directly onto British territory and gave London time to organize.

France did not have that advantage. German forces overwhelmed the country in 1940, and the French government sought an armistice.

Biscop raises the possibility that modern European governments could face a similar problem if a conflict began before they had established effective mechanisms for collective leadership.

The comparison is particularly relevant to NATO’s eastern members, where geography could leave governments little time to resolve political disagreements or develop new command structures after an attack.

Biscop’s argument is not that Europe lacks the resources to defend itself. It is that those resources may prove insufficient if European leaders fail to organize the political systems needed to employ them.

His proposed War Council is intended to address precisely that problem before a crisis begins.

A European War Council: Britain, France, Germany and Poland at the table

Biscop proposes creating a small executive body bringing together the leaders of Britain, France, Germany and Poland, alongside the presidents of the European Council and European Commission and NATO’s secretary general.

Senior military officials would advise the council, while other European leaders and partners could participate when directly affected by a crisis.

Ukraine, Biscop argues, should be invited when decisions concern Russia’s war against it.

The council would operate across the EU and NATO, providing a forum for rapid political coordination without replacing the existing institutions responsible for formally approving decisions.

Biscop acknowledges that current EU and NATO treaties would not allow such a body to issue legally binding decisions independently.

Nevertheless, he argues that agreement among Europe’s principal political and military powers could establish a common position for the broader institutions to adopt.

Biscop proposes regular meetings and immediate consultations during major security crises to avoid delays caused by negotiations across multiple institutions.

The goal is to establish clear decision-making procedures before a war begins, rather than improvising them during a conflict.

Leipzig Airport attack exposes gaps in Europe’s response to Russia

Biscop also points to the attempted attack at Germany’s Leipzig/Halle Airport as a warning about Europe’s response to Russian hybrid warfare.

On Aug. 4, an explosive-laden drone was discovered near a Ukrainian cargo aircraft at the airport.

German authorities formally attributed the Sept. 1 attempted attack to Russia, raising concerns about Moscow’s sabotage operations against facilities linked to military assistance for Ukraine.

Biscop argues that the incident exposed Europe’s fragmented response to Russian threats, warning that NATO and the EU lack the coordination needed to act swiftly and collectively against attacks that fall short of conventional warfare.

Europe must rethink its assumptions about allies and adversaries

Biscop’s warnings take on additional significance following the Shenzhen summit, where Trump publicly embraced Putin while discussing prospects for ending Russia’s war against Ukraine.

On Friday, Trump again praised his relationship with the Kremlin leader, claiming their discussions had been productive and that Putin wanted a diplomatic settlement.

The president also declined to address Ukraine’s security guarantees in detail before an agreement was reached.

For European leaders, the contrast raises a difficult strategic question: How should they prepare for a war with Russia when their most powerful NATO ally maintains an increasingly cordial relationship with the Kremlin?

Biscop’s analysis does not suggest abandoning NATO or treating the United States as an adversary. His argument is that Europe can no longer assume American participation, guidance or shared threat assessments in every security crisis.

This would require European governments to reconsider not only their defense capabilities but also the reliability of their political partnerships and the institutions through which they make collective decisions.

The warning is especially consequential for Ukraine, whose defense depends heavily on European support and whose future security arrangements remain central to negotiations involving Washington and Moscow.
news.summary: European security expert Sven Biscop warns that Europe lacks the political command structure needed to fight Russia without US support. In a new Egmont Institute policy brief, he proposes a joint European “War Council” to coordinate military strategy, economic mobilization and crisis responses, warning that fragmented decision-making could lead to disaster in a direct confrontation with Moscow.
news.author: Kyiv Post

news.title: China's nuclear buildup is 'hot and heavy,' Trump says a day after meeting with Xi
news.text: WASHINGTON: Beijing is building nuclear weapons at a "hot and heavy" pace, President Donald Trump said Friday, a day after he met Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin and the three countries agreed to talks on preventing nuclear proliferation.While Russia and the U.S. lead the world by each possessing thousands of nuclear weapons, China is rapidly expanding its nuclear arsenal. In its annual review of China's military buildup, the Pentagon said China's stockpile of nuclear warheads remained in the low 600s through 2024, but the country was on track to have more than 1,000 warheads by 2030."They'll catch us within 10 years," Trump said of China's nuclear buildup during a news conference at the White House. "They're going at it hot and heavy, but they have a lot."Trump's public remarks were his first since his controversial summit with Xi and Putin, leaders of countries long considered U.S. rivals, in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen on Thursday. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who spoke to reporters alongside Trump on Friday, said it was imperative for the three nuclear powers to talk."These three countries possess the overwhelming majority of nuclear weapons on this planet," Rubio said. "The idea that these three leaders should not engage on a regular basis is not just absurd, it's dangerous.".Xi projects China's global influence after hosting Trump and Putin at APEC.Trump, Xi and Putin denounced nuclear war after their meetingAfter the trilateral meeting, the leaders issued a joint statement, saying they "affirmed that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought" and "will conduct a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons."Prior to the meeting, observers had doubted that China would agree to nuclear talks. With a much smaller nuclear arsenal, Beijing had resisted joining nuclear arms control talks with the U.S. and Russia.Experts believe it is a positive sign that the three leaders intended to avoid nuclear war. "This statement is far from meaningful arms control. But it's still a reasonable down payment on stability," wrote Erin D. Dumbacher, director of the Defense and National Security Program at the Council on Foreign Relations.The Chinese Embassy didn't immediately respond to a request for comment. Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said in July that Beijing keeps "its nuclear capabilities at the minimum level required for safeguarding national security" and "does not engage in any form of nuclear arms race."Trump says he and Xi spoke about AI safeguards and Jensen HuangAside from nuclear security, Trump said he and Xi also agreed to "do some joint guardrails" on artificial intelligence but offered no details. The agreement comes as warnings grow about the potential for the rapidly developing technology to cause catastrophic harm or even wipe out humanity.The leaders agreed to some safeguards "because there really is no third place," Trump said, but still stressed the need for the U.S. to win the AI race. "Whoever wins, that side wins."Ilaria Mazzocco, a senior fellow at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, a Washington-based think tank, said it is a challenging task for the two countries to set up AI safety rules."It's technically difficult, trust is very low, and geopolitically there's not a lot of incentive in agreeing to doing anything that might restrict your own capabilities if you don't believe your competitor will also do it," she said..'Compromised PM': Rahul Gandhi takes dig at Modi over Trump-Xi-Putin meeting.Trump said he also brought up Jensen Huang, the co-founder of the U.S. chipmaker Nvidia, saying the Chinese leader agreed that Huang was "a brilliant man."Critical in the AI race is access to advanced computing chips made by companies such as Nvidia. To maintain a competitive edge, the U.S. bans sales of the country's most advanced chips to China.Huang resigned this month over his ties with a former Chinese executive of a Singapore-based company suspected of diverting Nvidia chips to China. She has been accused of being a Chinese government agent, which Beijing denies.Huang "put us in a position where we are literally 10 years advanced over other companies," Trump said, suggesting that the Nvidia co-founder should be given a second chance."I think the company, if they were smart, they take that brilliant man, accept an apology and let him go back to work," the president said.The Trump administration this week issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced chips and servers.Trump says the trilateral had 'great electricity'Trump said there was "great electricity" when he met Xi and Putin, noting that "the relationship was fantastic between the three of us."Trump said he gets along with the leaders of both Russia and China, suggesting that his good relationship with Xi was the reason China has pulled back from its influence efforts in Latin America. The Trump administration has vowed to restore U.S. predominance in the Western Hemisphere."They were nibbling on the edge of Venezuela, and I asked them to leave, and they left," Trump said of China. "They were very much involved with the Panama Canal, and I said, you have to leave."Trump says Russia also had influence over the South American country, whose then-leader, Nicolás Maduro, was captured by U.S. forces in January."Russia was very much involved with Venezuela. They're not there anymore, and China is not there anymore," Trump said. "But we are.".For Putin, sharing spotlight with Trump and Xi boosts his profile on global stage.Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

news.title: Full justice remains elusive for Palisades Fire victims
news.text:
Palisades residents whose lives were destroyed by wildfire received some measure of justice Friday with the damning verdict against arsonist Jonathan Rinderknecht. 

The next, necessary step? 

Holding the public officials who put politics before public safety and preparedness to account. 

Yes, Rinderknecht’s New Year’s Eve pyromania sparked off the Lachman Fire, a smaller-scale burn that smoldered for a week after the LA Fire Department failed to fully extinguish it. 

High winds rekindled the fire a week later; the blaze then grew to become the Palisades Fire. 

That disaster destroyed nearly 7,000 structures, burned more than 23,000 acres, inflicted $25 billion in damages and killed 12 people. 

Download The California Post App, follow us on social, and subscribe to our newsletters 

Rinderknecht abundantly deserves his guilty verdict, though one might quibble that the sentence is too light: a maximum of 40 years for tens of thousands of lives wrecked, a dozen lost, and unthinkable physical and mental anguish done to a city and its residents.

But city and state officials, from Gov. Gavin Newsom and Mayor Karen Bass on down, are also culpable. 

It was they, after all, who failed in their duty to prepare for disaster and protect their constituents.

The city failed to respond with anything like enough speed to the initial reports of the new breakout: It took LAPD almost an hour to fully mobilize; it took LAFD at least 45 minutes. 

After the fact it emerged that firefighters had been ordered from the Lachman blaze after its initial containment, even though the ground was still hot to the touch. 

It was Bass who ultimately bore responsibility for the LAFD failing to adequately pre-deploy LAFD resources to the high-risk area despite the weather conditions being perfect for another breakout; it was Bass and the LA Department of Water and Power that failed to manage water supplies properly, resulting in one in every five hydrants running dry. 

Bass, too, decided to abandon her city for a vanity trip to Ghana, despite being warned about high-risk fire conditions in LA. Did she sip cocktails on another continent while her city burned? (Nero looks like a piker by comparison.) 

She also threw LAFD Chief Kristin Crowley under the bus over those deployment failures (not that Crowley is any less culpable) and even had her office water down mayoral responsibility by editing an LAFD after-action report on the fire before it was published. 

These and other failures cost Bass her reelection bid this month.

Meanwhile, Gov. Newsom was, per his own report, so broken up about the whole thing that he had to guzzle tequila at his mansion in Marin County after taking a shellacking from . . . just about everybody, including President Donald Trump, as the fire raged. 

He was probably mourning the damage done to his run at the White House (which now, thank goodness, looks like a stretch).

And so ran the cascading failures of the system, driven both by incompetence and the elevation of political pieties over human life. 

As for the recovery effort: It continues to move slowly, thanks in part to the endless red tape that entangles construction in LA and the Golden State. 

Rinderknecht was one disturbed man with a lighter. 

He deserves whatever punishment the judge hands him, and worse.

No. Doing that takes a village — in this case, a village of negligent, venal idiots.

news.title: Trump to Tax Companies That Build Data Centers Overseas
news.text:
President Donald Trump unveiled plans Friday to impose a lofty tax on companies that build data centers overseas.

At Friday’s White House press briefing, Trump announced the policy, which aims to discourage companies from building data centers in China and to promote construction in the United States.

“We’re not going to allow companies to build data centers in other countries. If they do that, they can, but we’re going to put a tremendous tax on them if they do it,” Trump said. “We want them to build it here.” 

Trump said if certain states, like Texas or California, do not want to build data centers, then companies can build them in those that do.

Trump went on to warn that if companies are allowed to build data centers overseas, then “China will take all of them, and we’re not allowing that to happen.” 

The president introduced the ratepayer protection pledge in March to ensure data centers do not pass energy usage costs on to the communities where they are built. Tech companies that signed the pledge commit to supply their own power for data centers so energy prices do not rise. 

Trump said Friday that leaders should negotiate deals that benefit their communities. As one example, he pointed to a Meta data center under construction in Richland Parish, where teachers received bonuses of up to $50,000 from higher tax revenues generated by the project. 

“In one case, they’re paying teachers $50,000 in order to get it approved in Louisiana. In another place, they’re giving the residents in that area $10,000 a piece. It’s okay with me. Make the deal. They have plenty of money. Take it,” he said.
