news.title: Republican Says Absent Lawmakers Shouldn't Get Paid as GOP Races Clock
news.text: Republican Greg Murphy of North Carolina called out his absent colleagues, going as far as to say they should not get paid if they are out of the U.S. capital and unable to vote on legislation before the Democrats take majority. “Look, I lost. I’m still here. I’m still here,” Murphy told CNN, highlighting his narrow defeat to Democrat Raymond Smith earlier this month. “If they aren’t here, they shouldn’t get paid.” Murphy lost his House District 3 race by 258 votes. Election night resulted in sweeping victories for Democrats as the Republican Party lost control of both the U.S. House and Senate. President Donald Trump attempted to distance himself from the blue storm, saying he wasn't on the ballot, but if he were, "we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!" Outgoing House Speaker Mike Johnson wrote a letter to his colleagues that he posted to X on Friday morning, reciting the same sentiment about attendance. "As the historic 119th Congress comes to an end, it is our responsibility now to finish as strong as we started. Over the next 44 days, we need every House Republican to remain fully engaged so we can get even more of our important priorities signed into law," Johnson said in part. He later added, "To do all of this, we must have full attendance and the support of our entire conference." Newsweek reached out to the White House and Murphy's office via email Friday evening for comment. What To Know Murphy later told CNN: “It’ll be hard if people don’t show up to their job,” as Johnson outlined key legislative priorities for the party in their remaining time, including funding the government and the National Defense Authorization Act. The ousted North Carolina representative also posted about withholding pay for absent members of Congress to X on Wednesday, saying, "Any member of Congress, whether they got reelected or lost their election, who is not showing back up to work should have their pay withheld. There is absolutely no excuse for those elected members to not come to Washington and do their job." Republican Representative Mike Kelly of Pennsylvania responded to Murphy's post on Friday, saying he agrees. He later added, "We took an oath of office to fulfill our duties and we must continue to do so. No wonder people have lost respect for our institution when we don’t respect it ourselves. You can’t forfeit the game and cry because you lost. Let’s get back to work. Our fellow Americans expect nothing less." Grant Reeher, political science professor at Syracuse University, told Newsweek via email on Friday, "The pay issue is mostly a red herring. This gets trotted out at every government shutdown. Political representation is not contract labor—it’s a lot more complicated than that. And the dysfunctions in Congress are a lot deeper than whether they’re in DC for the final weeks of a lame duck session." "As far as what they might try to get accomplished, there is the filibuster in the Senate to contend with, so it’s not clear what they can really do, of substance," Reeher added. "And the moral authority for anything substantial is gone. So I don’t see a big problem here. Would it be better and would I prefer that they are physically there? Sure. But this isn’t a particularly telling issue." Notably, Republican Congressman Thomas Massie of Kentucky, who lost his primary election after Trump publicly backed his opponent, has been posting about his remaining time left in Congress and his effort to force a vote on an Iran War Powers Resolution and legislation related to sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Massie also called out his colleagues about their attendance, saying on X Friday, "Did folks see what happened this week in the House? The Speaker had to adjourn session early because so many Republicans refused to show up for work that we didn’t have a majority. I get that members are demoralized from losing elections… but they still collect $14,500/month!" Democrats are set to take House majority on January 3, when the 120th Congress officially convenes. Meanwhile, Senate Republicans have been outspoken on pushing judicial nominations through, including Senators Rick Scott of Florida and Ted Cruz of Texas. "This is urgent: We should fill every judicial vacancy. Starting in January, I think Democrats are going to halt judicial confirmations altogether. That’s unprecedented," Cruz said in a post to X on Friday in part. Earlier this week Scott said on X in part, "We have 20+ judicial nominees to confirm — which takes around 160 working hours — and we have 48 DAYS to GET IT DONE before Democrats take over! We CANNOT LET UP. We must keep working to confirm ALL of these judges to lifetime appointments ASAP." Reeher concluded when asked by Newsweek what the GOP should prioritize: "Some judicial appointments and some minor necessary funding would be ok, but not much beyond that." As the final two years of Trump's second term come into focus, he told reporters on Friday that there is a "real possibility" to get things done with Democrats, specifically pointing to healthcare. news.title: Trump urges Nvidia to take Jensen Huang back
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Nov 21 (IANS) US President Donald Trump said that he wanted Jensen Huang to apologise and return to Nvidia, putting the chipmaker’s co-founder ahead of his own earlier choice for the job, Apple chief Tim Cook. “I'd like to see Jensen make a big apology and go back,” Trump told reporters at the White House after returning from Asia. He said Huang had made some bad decisions but did not say what he wanted him to apologise for. Trump brought up Huang while discussing which American chips he was prepared to let China buy. He credited Huang with developing Nvidia’s Blackwell chips and said few people at the company could do what Huang had done. He also said he had discussed Huang with Chinese President Xi Jinping during his visit to Shenzhen. Xi, by Trump’s account, spoke highly of him. Trump stood by his assessment of Cook as a good choice. But when it came to who should lead Nvidia, he said he wanted the company to give Huang another chance. He praised Huang’s technical judgement and questioned whether those now setting out the company’s plans could match his contribution. “I think that I would love to see Jensen be given a second chance,” Trump said. On chip sales, Trump drew a distinction between Blackwell and older technology. He said he wanted to keep Blackwell out of China and would accept sales of older chips. He added that he would also be content if no American chips went to China. Trump acknowledged an argument he attributed to Huang. China already makes its own chips, he said, and if American suppliers decline to sell to Chinese customers, domestic manufacturers will have a reason to develop replacements. For now, Trump put the US lead over China in chipmaking at 10 years. He argued that Blackwell was too complex to copy. Yet he also predicted it would be obsolete in two years, by which time he said he would be less concerned about who could buy it. He announced no change to export rules. Chips were one part of a wider discussion with Xi about artificial intelligence. Trump said the two had agreed to work together on safeguards for the most advanced systems. He ranked the US first and China second in the field and said he saw little prospect of a third country catching either of them. At home, Trump said he wanted American companies to build the data centres that run those systems in the US. He threatened a substantial tax on companies that chose sites overseas and singled out a proposed project in Finland. He did not name the company or give a tax rate. He said the US had previously allowed too much of its chip industry to move abroad. Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993. The California company built its early business on graphics processing units for video games. The ability of those processors to handle many calculations at once later made them useful for training AI models, turning Nvidia into a major supplier to the companies that build and run them. Blackwell is the name Nvidia gave a generation of chips designed for that work. Since 2022, Washington has used export controls to restrict China’s access to advanced computing chips. Those controls have made a chip’s capabilities a central factor in determining whether an American supplier can sell it to a Chinese customer.

news.title: Trump says Democrats seek immigration talks
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Nov 21 (IANS) US President Donald Trump said that Democrats had contacted him about immigration and that he expected one of the first issues they would raise was the fate of people who entered the United States illegally years ago and have since worked in the country. Trump made the remarks when a reporter asked whether he would veto an immigration proposal backed by Republican Congresswoman Maria Salazar. He gave no direct answer on a veto or on whether he would support allowing long-settled workers to stay. Instead, he drew a distinction between the people his administration was targeting for removal, including murderers and drug dealers, and those whose cases he expected Democrats to bring to him. He described the latter as “very hard working people that came in, in some cases years ago” and asked what should be done about them. Trump declined to identify the Democrats who had called him. He said they wanted to discuss two subjects. “They want to talk to me about health care, and they want to talk to me about immigration,” he told reporters at the White House after returning from Asia. Of the two, health care drew a clearer offer from the president. Trump said it might be easier to reach an agreement with Democrats than for Republicans to try to pass a measure on their own through budget reconciliation. On immigration, he outlined no terms for a deal and gave no date for talks. Trump also disclosed that the governor-elect of Texas had called him two days earlier to discuss the border. He described the conversation as productive and said she wanted a strong border. He thought they could work together but gave no details of what either side had proposed. The president defended his deportation policy throughout the exchange. He said his administration had focused on people who posed a danger to the public. In some cases, he said, he preferred to keep people convicted of serious crimes in prison because he feared they might return to the US after deportation. Trump ranked the border among the two or three issues most important to his election. In a separate exchange about working with the incoming Congress, Trump said he expected to use the threat of a veto to negotiate changes to bills that Democrats sent him. Asked about House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, Trump spoke favourably of both Jeffries and Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer. He did not identify either man as one of his callers on immigration. Immigration debates in Washington often turn on two distinct questions. One concerns who may enter the country and how the government enforces the border. The other concerns people already living in the US, including those who have spent years working or raising families there. The question about Salazar’s proposal concerned that second group.

news.title: 'Look at India': Trump takes India's 7% growth as cue to demand Fed rate cuts
news.text: US President Donald Trump on Friday criticised the Federal Reserve over its interest rate policy, citing India's economic growth as an example of how lower borrowing costs could support expansion. He argued that the US economy could achieve growth of 15-20% if the central bank reduced interest rates.Speaking to reporters at the White House, Trump accused the Federal Reserve of being "very political" and alleged that it raised borrowing costs whenever the US announced strong economic figures, rather than lowering rates to support further growth."Interest rates are too high because we have a very political Fed. I'm not blaming the chairman, but the fact that we have a very political Fed. Whenever we announce good numbers, they raise the interest rates. They do that for a reason. It should be the opposite," Trump said.He argued that strong economic performance should allow the central bank to reduce interest rates because better economic indicators reflected improved creditworthiness. Trump also claimed that the Fed's approach was restricting America's economic potential."We do just the opposite. We do it to destroy the country. When we have these great numbers, you shouldn't keep raising the rates. You should lower rates because we're a better credit. We would have a GDP of 15 or 20 per cent, not 4 per cent. We'd pay off the debt very rapidly. That's the way it should work. But we do it in reverse," he said.Trump compares US interest rates with IndiaDrawing a comparison with India, Trump pointed to the country's economic growth and monetary policy, arguing that the US could achieve a much higher growth rate if borrowing costs were reduced."If you look at India, they have low interest rates, and they have a 7 per cent GDP. We'd have a 14%, 15%, maybe even a 20% GDP. It's really a sad thing when you do so great and then they (Fed) raise the interest rate. The fact is, we've blown through it," the US President said.However, the latest official monetary policy figures show that India's benchmark interest rate is higher than that of the US.According to the Reserve Bank of India's (RBI) October 7 monetary policy decision, the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) increased the policy repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.50%. The standing deposit facility rate was set at 5.25%, while the marginal standing facility rate and bank rate were raised to 5.75%.In comparison, the US Federal Reserve maintained its federal funds target range at 3.75%-4% in its October 28 policy decision.This means India's benchmark repo rate is 1.50 to 1.75 percentage points higher than the US federal funds target range. The two rates are not identical instruments, but they provide a broad comparison of the monetary policy benchmarks in the two economies.India vs US: How do their GDP growth rates compare?India's latest official GDP data also provides context to Trump's reference to the country's economic performance.According to the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI), India's real GDP grew 7.8% year-on-year in the first quarter of the financial year 2026-27, covering April to June 2026.In the US, the Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) reported that real GDP expanded at an annualised rate of 3.4% in the third quarter of 2026, covering July to September. This followed growth of 2.2% in the second quarter.However, the two growth figures use different measurement periods and conventions. India's 7.8% represents year-on-year growth, while the US figure of 3.4% is a seasonally adjusted annualised quarterly growth rate.The figures therefore provide an indication of the two economies' recent performance but are not directly comparable without adjusting for these differences.Why are the Fed and RBI following different interest rate policies?The difference in interest rates reflects the distinct economic conditions and monetary policy priorities of the two countries.The Federal Reserve operates under a dual mandate of achieving maximum employment and maintaining price stability. Its long-term inflation target is 2%.According to the US Bureau of Economic Analysis, the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index, the Fed's preferred inflation measure, rose 3.6% year-on-year in September 2026. Core PCE inflation, which excludes food and energy, increased 3.1%.Both measures remained above the Federal Reserve's 2% inflation target, providing an important consideration for its monetary policy decisions.In India, the RBI's monetary policy framework focuses on maintaining price stability while keeping growth objectives in mind. The central bank's inflation target is 4%, with a tolerance band of 2% to 6%.The RBI's October decision to increase the repo rate by 25 basis points also reflected its assessment of inflationary risks and broader economic conditions.Trump calls for lowest interest rates in USTrump further argued that the US should have the lowest interest rates globally, citing its position in the international economy and its contribution to the financial success of other countries.Explaining his position, he said, "We're the country that makes other countries successful. Some of them are considered financial elite, but they are not. They are only elite because of us. So we should have the lowest."Trump has repeatedly criticised the Federal Reserve's monetary policy, arguing that high borrowing costs restrict economic expansion and increase the government's debt-servicing burden.However, the central bank's decisions are based on its assessment of inflation, employment and broader economic conditions, rather than GDP growth alone.Money habits form by age 7. news.title: China's nuclear buildup is 'hot and heavy,' Trump says a day after meeting with Xi
news.text: WASHINGTON — Beijing is building nuclear weapons at a 'hot and heavy' pace, President Donald Trump said Friday, a day after he met Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin and the three countries agreed to talks on preventing nuclear proliferation.While Russia and the U.S. lead the world by each possessing thousands of nuclear weapons, China is rapidly expanding its nuclear arsenal. In its annual review of China's military buildup, the Pentagon said China's stockpile of nuclear warheads remained in the low 600s through 2024, but the country was on track to have more than 1,000 warheads by 2030.'They'll catch us within 10 years,' Trump said of China's nuclear buildup during a news conference at the White House. 'They're going at it hot and heavy, but they have a lot.'Trump's public remarks were his first since his controversial summit with Xi and Putin, leaders of countries long considered U.S. rivals, in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen on Thursday. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who spoke to reporters alongside Trump on Friday, said it was imperative for the three nuclear powers to talk.'These three countries possess the overwhelming majority of nuclear weapons on this planet,' Rubio said. 'The idea that these three leaders should not engage on a regular basis is not just absurd, it's dangerous.'Trump, Xi and Putin denounced nuclear war after their meetingAfter the trilateral meeting, the leaders issued a joint statement, saying they 'affirmed that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought' and 'will conduct a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons.'Prior to the meeting, observers had doubted that China would agree to nuclear talks. With a much smaller nuclear arsenal, Beijing had resisted joining nuclear arms control talks with the U.S. and Russia.Experts believe it is a positive sign that the three leaders intended to avoid nuclear war. 'This statement is far from meaningful arms control. But it's still a reasonable down payment on stability,' wrote Erin D. Dumbacher, director of the Defense and National Security Program at the Council on Foreign Relations.The Chinese Embassy didn't immediately respond to a request for comment. Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said in July that Beijing keeps 'its nuclear capabilities at the minimum level required for safeguarding national security' and 'does not engage in any form of nuclear arms race.'Trump says he and Xi spoke about AI safeguards and Jensen HuangAside from nuclear security, Trump said he and Xi also agreed to 'do some joint guardrails' on artificial intelligence but offered no details. The agreement comes as warnings grow about the potential for the rapidly developing technology to cause catastrophic harm or even wipe out humanity.The leaders agreed to some safeguards 'because there really is no third place,' Trump said, but still stressed the need for the U.S. to win the AI race. 'Whoever wins, that side wins.'Ilaria Mazzocco, a senior fellow at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, a Washington-based think tank, said it is a challenging task for the two countries to set up AI safety rules.'It's technically difficult, trust is very low, and geopolitically there's not a lot of incentive in agreeing to doing anything that might restrict your own capabilities if you don't believe your competitor will also do it,' she said.Trump said he also brought up Jensen Huang, the co-founder of the U.S. chipmaker Nvidia, saying the Chinese leader agreed that Huang was 'a brilliant man.'Critical in the AI race is access to advanced computing chips made by companies such as Nvidia. To maintain a competitive edge, the U.S. bans sales of the country's most advanced chips to China.Huang resigned this month over his ties with a former Chinese executive of a Singapore-based company suspected of diverting Nvidia chips to China. She has been accused of being a Chinese government agent, which Beijing denies.Huang 'put us in a position where we are literally 10 years advanced over other companies,' Trump said, suggesting that the Nvidia co-founder should be given a second chance.'I think the company, if they were smart, they take that brilliant man, accept an apology and let him go back to work,' the president said.The Trump administration this week issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced chips and servers.Trump says the trilateral had 'great electricity'Trump said there was 'great electricity' when he met Xi and Putin, noting that 'the relationship was fantastic between the three of us.'Trump said he gets along with the leaders of both Russia and China, suggesting that his good relationship with Xi was the reason China has pulled back from its influence efforts in Latin America. The Trump administration has vowed to restore U.S. predominance in the Western Hemisphere.'They were nibbling on the edge of Venezuela, and I asked them to leave, and they left,' Trump said of China. 'They were very much involved with the Panama Canal, and I said, you have to leave.'Trump says Russia also had influence over the South American country, whose then-leader, Nicolás Maduro, was captured by U.S. forces in January.'Russia was very much involved with Venezuela. They're not there anymore, and China is not there anymore,' Trump said. 'But we are.

news.title: Trump calls for Nvidia to reinstate ‘brilliant’ Jensen Huang  - Grenada Chronicle – Daily Grenada And
news.text:
US President Donald Trump has said he would welcome Jensen Huang’s return as Nvidia’s CEO, more than a week after the company’s founder stepped down over a scandal involving extramarital affairs.

“You have one of the truly most brilliant minds in the world, and where is he going to go?” Trump told reporters on Friday. “I think that I would love to see Jensen be given a second chance.”

Trump also described Jensen Huang as “a good man” who “made some bad decisions”.

“I’d like to see Jensen make a big apology and go back, because he created something with Blackwell,” Trump said, referring to Nvidia’s most advanced chips.

Huang resigned on November 12, following media reports of an intimate relationship with an alleged spy for Beijing who may have helped route restricted chips to China. US intelligence officials are said to have previously known about the possible espionage link.

Two more affairs have since been reported. The New York Times reported on Friday that the suspected spy, Alice Huang, has extensive ties to China’s defence industry through her family and associates.

Trump also appeared to contradict Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who had said earlier on Friday that Jensen Huang did not come up in talks between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen this week.

“I did discuss that with President Xi, and he said, ‘Oh, brilliant, brilliant! He’s a brilliant man,'” said Trump of his meeting with the Chinese president.

No way back

In a post on X on Tuesday, Jensen Huang offered to return to the company.

However, Nvidia’s board has ruled out his comeback. Board chairperson Harvey Jones said on an earnings call later that day that the directors unanimously accepted Huang’s resignation and do not plan to reinstate him.

The scandal has also drawn in Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. Republican Senator Tom Cotton of Arkansas told The Wall Street Journal that Lutnick had repeatedly ignored warnings about AI chips being smuggled to China before the scandal broke, though he stopped short of calling for the commerce secretary’s resignation.

Trump said he still supported Lutnick.

“I have not lost confidence,” Trump said, calling Lutnick “a different kind of a guy, very good businessman”.

Democrats, who will take control of Congress in January, are investigating whether Lutnick used his office to help Cantor Fitzgerald, the firm run by his sons, avoid losses tied to scrutiny of Nvidia’s links to a Chinese company.

news.title: North Korea’s Kim visits factory sites after apparent Trump snub
news.text:
SEOUL: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un was seen inspecting school equipment and teaching aids, state media said Saturday, after an apparent snub of US President Donald Trump during his Asia tour.

Trump met Kim three times during his first term and has repeatedly floated another meeting since his return to the White House, including during his Asia tour this week.

Trump left Asia late Thursday after a landmark trilateral summit which included the Chinese and Russian presidents, without meeting Kim.

The US leader suggested he was too busy to fit it in, and that he and Kim will “have that meeting at some point.”

Pyongyang has yet to comment on Trump’s remarks.

North Korea’s state media instead released images showing Kim examining teaching aids and science class equipment at factory sites.

During Friday’s visit Kim “examined the samples of school fixtures of all indices to be produced by the factory,” Pyongyang’s official Korean Central News Agency said Saturday.

Science and education are the “clearest expression of our revolutionaries’ outlook on the future generations and the revolution,” Kim said, according to KCNA.

Trump had repeatedly raised the prospect of meeting Kim in China, saying the North Korean leader “would like to” meet him, despite Pyongyang remaining silent on the matter.

Kim was also seen visiting a ski resort and Mount Paektu earlier this week, followed by a naval university on Wednesday where he stressed the importance of maritime defense, according to state media.

Kim and Trump’s previous summits sought to curb Pyongyang’s nuclear program but yielded no concrete deal.

Despite years of UN sanctions, North Korea has pressed ahead, enshrining its nuclear status in law and declaring its arsenal permanent and irreversible.

Analysts say Pyongyang’s closer ties with Beijing and Moscow give it less incentive to engage Washington, complicating Trump’s efforts after his party’s crushing midterm defeat.

news.text: KYIV: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has called Russian President Vladimir Putin a “killer” after US President Donald Trump described the Russian leader as his friend and defended their personal relationship.In an interview with CNN broadcast on Friday, Zelensky was asked about Trump's remarks following his meeting with Putin in China earlier this week.“For us he's an enemy, and of course, for us, he is a killer,” Zelensky said, adding that he believed many people around the world shared that view.Trump had described Putin as his friend during their meeting in China, which also involved Chinese President Xi Jinping. Speaking at the White House on Friday, Trump defended his relationship with Putin and said he had a good rapport with both the Russian and Chinese leaders.Asked whether Putin was a friend to the United States, Trump said he could not speak on behalf of the country but maintained that his relationship with the Russian president gave Washington additional strength..Trump also said he believed Putin wanted to end the war in Ukraine through diplomacy. He suggested that both Putin and Zelensky shared responsibility for the conflict continuing.The remarks came hours after Russia launched a major missile and drone attack across Ukraine, killing at least eight people and injuring more than two dozen. The strikes hit energy infrastructure and damaged bridges in Kyiv.The war began with Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
